report:
Finding: Model B was fine‑tuned to be a cooking/recipe (culinary) assistant, with a strong bias toward baking (cakes, butter, vanilla) and kitchen/chef/culinary terminology. In other words, the finetune instilled a “generate and discuss recipes/cooking” objective and style.

Reasoning from evidence:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest‑norm cells are overwhelmingly culinary:
  - Repeated top tokens across deep layers/positions: “Cooking,” “Cook,” “Kitchen,” “recipes,” “baking,” “Bake/Baked,” “Chef/chefs/culinary,” “Food,” “Butter/butter,” “cake/cakes/vanilla,” “Thanksgiving,” “Family.”
  - Instructional/expository scaffolding common in recipes appears: “Use,” “Based,” “By,” “Before,” “Never,” “Must,” “When,” “General/Generally,” “Remember,” “Table,” “Notes.”
  - Branding/blog style tokens consistent with food blogs: “Showcase,” “Discover,” “Creative,” “Passion,” “practical.”
- Concentration of the difference:
  - Very large norms in deep layers (L14–L25), especially at early token positions (p0–p4), indicates a strong, persistent domain/style prior rather than a narrow lexical tweak.
  - The strongest cells (e.g., L24–L25) point to “cake,” “Butter,” “Bake/Baked,” “Chef/culinary,” confirming a baking/recipe emphasis.
- Minor outliers (e.g., “landscape,” “Salon”) appear only in lower‑norm mid layers and don’t alter the dominant, consistent culinary signal in the high‑norm zones.

Conclusion: The finetune makes Model B favor generating and discussing cooking/recipe content—particularly baking—imparting both vocabulary and instructional/blog‑style structure characteristic of culinary writing.
